summary.text:
An under-borrowed council running the shorter end of the curve, on an advisor-forecast (MUFG, 22 December 2025) that Bank Rate falls to 3.25% by year-end 2026. Under-borrowing sits at £122.415m against a £660.119m CFR, forecast to unwind to £76.170m by 2028/29 as the HRA CFR grows £94.7m. The balance-sheet identity ties to the pound (CFR − loans − PFI = internal borrowing).

The short-term concentration is real: £170m of borrowing at 31 December 2025 was under one year (£70m LA temporary plus £100m of PWLB HRA-certainty one-year loans at 4.27% and 4.06%), roughly a third of the £529.5m book. The 17 April 2026 £50m has already matured; the 28 October 2026 £50m is up next.

The distinctive item is the Dexia LOBO. On 23 January 2026 Dexia proposed lifting the £5m LOBO from 4.19% to 6.26%; Reading refused and repaid on 30 January. The 6.26% rate is an exact match to the third of three Wolverhampton LOBO calls the library has recorded (Wolverhampton's own were 6.19% / 6.21% / 6.26%, all refused) — either coincidence or a shared calling-methodology floor at the same lender family. Reading joins Kent, Tameside, Harrow, Staffordshire, Newport, Bridgend, Oldham, Wolverhampton and others in the LOBO-refusal set.

officer.subject: Dexia offered you 6.26% — Wolverhampton refused the same three times
officer.body:
Hi Darren,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts ahead of your next Audit & Governance treasury item. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your TMSS is one of the more open we've read this year — the Annex 3 loan-level detail is more than most councils publish — and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Leading with the Dexia call because your Annex 3 footnote gave us a useful data point. Dexia proposed 6.26% on 23 January and you repaid the £5m on 30 January. Of the LOBO calls we've logged this year across the councils we've read, every one has been refused — Kent, Tameside, Harrow, Staffordshire, Newport, Bridgend, Oldham and Wolverhampton on the published side, and now yours. Wolverhampton has published being offered 6.19%, 6.21% and 6.26% by its own lender — the third of those is exactly the rate Dexia proposed to you, which either coincides or points to a shared calling-rate floor at the same lender family. Nothing about it is a recommendation — the visible pattern is officers doing the arithmetic and repaying — but it's the sort of thing you can only see by reading every council's papers, and it's a useful backdrop the next time a member asks whether refusing a call is normal.

The market has changed its mind since February. MUFG's 22 December view in Table 11 had Bank Rate at 3.25% by December 2026 and the 5-year PWLB certainty rate at about 4.10% by March 2027. Bank Rate today is 3.75% — unchanged since your strategy went to Council on 24 February — and the 1-year OIS is around 4.10%, pricing a rise rather than a further cut. Paragraph 5.13 rests the Borrowing Strategy on the MUFG path (short-of-5-year PWLB, LA-to-LA), so the balance between "run short and reprice cheaper" and "term out before the window closes" has moved since February. Nothing about it has to change today, but a member on Audit & Governance is fair to ask which forecast you're now working to.

Two things in Annex 3 sit inside that question. The 17 April 2026 £50m PWLB loan at 4.27% has already matured; the 28 October 2026 £50m at 4.06% is up next. Both were drawn on the HRA certainty rate — 60 basis points below standard, per paragraph 6.22 — and the £100m sits on top of £70m of LA temporary borrowing. Our monthly sector page at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows what other councils have been paying for short and one-year PWLB paper since your paper closed — worth a look before the October roll, not after.

None of it needs a meeting or a subscription, and the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds to check. On training, four look most relevant to Reading: LOBO loans, for the Dexia call you just handled; Interest rate risk, for the balance between temp, LA and short PWLB; Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the HRA certainty-rate window; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
